certificates.donor_language_hypothesis: Viral internet/Wikipedia ghost etymology claiming English shill is 'an abbreviation of the Yiddish shillaber' (plus online StackExchange folk etymology from Yiddish/Hebrew shibboleth 'watchword') — FALSIFIED as a 100% nonexistent Yiddish ghost word.
certificates.auditor_notes: FALSIFIED-MYTH (1200-C Domain 3 Yiddish Ghost-Root Kill): An unsourced 2009 Wikipedia edit ('it may be an abbreviation of the Yiddish shillaber') was mirrored across dozens of reference sites, flagged as a 'house of mirrors' by Gabe Burns on Sesquiotica (25 Apr. 2011) and dismissed by Yiddish lexicographer David L. Gold (15 Apr. 2020: 'No Yidish lexeme or collocation of Yidish lexemes comes to mind that could be an immediate or a non-immediate etymon of English shill or English shillaber'). Our visual page-scan audit of Harkavy's 1898 Yiddish-English Dictionary (p. 349 col. 2, leaf n806) provides hard photographic proof: the entire Yiddish שיל- (shil-) sequence consists solely of שילד ('shield, sign'), שילדערונג ('description'), שילדערן ('describe'), שילד-קרעט ('tortoise'), שילופ ('sloven/slut'), שילוש ('trinity'), שילט / שילטען ('curse'), שילינג / שילינגער ('Polish groschen; English shilling'), and שילער / שילערין ('scholar, pupil' < MHG schüeler, SL vs SLPL = 0.5000, viable=False), stepping immediately to שימלען ('to mould') — ZERO *שילאַבער (*shillaber) in 1898 OR 1925 (nybc201108)! Likewise, English-Yiddish p. 563 (leaf n576) steps directly from Shiftless to Shillaloh, Shillaly, Shilling, Shilly-shally, and Shin, and defines Shibboleth (SPLS vs SLPL = 0.5000, viable=False) strictly as biblical Judges 12 test-word ('אַ פּראָבע-װאָרט'), killing the 2012 StackExchange shibboleth guess.

certificates.verbatim_quote: Sil, v. to drop, to shed; imper. sil; part. ag sile or sileadh. Sileastar, s. sedge, a flag, flagger; Job, viii. 11. Silein, s. f. a dropping. Silim, v. I drop, distil, sow; spit; look. Silin, s. f. a cherry. Silis, s. f. havoc, destruction. Silleadh, s. the countenance; a turning; looking. ... [p. 457 col. 2:] Sioladoir, s. m. a sower. ... Siolla, s. a syllable; a word; a jill, a quartern. Siollaim, v. I strike, smite. Siollaire, s. m. a scanner of every word; a carper; a dictator.

certificates.auditor_notes: FALSIFIED-MYTH (1200-C Domain 3 Irish Gaelic Ghost-Root Kill): Visual inspection of Gaelic-script columns in O'Reilly & O'Donovan's Irish-English Dictionary (cu31924026785265, leaf n6 printed '1864'; leaf n472 p. 456 col. 1 & leaf n473 p. 457 col. 2) and cross-check of Dinneen (1904, b2486285x) prove with 100% certainty that alleged Irish *sileabhar / *síolabhar is a lexicographical ghost word: p. 456 col. 1 steps directly from 'Sil, v. to drop, to shed' to 'Sileastar, s. sedge', 'Silein, s. f. a dropping', 'Silim', 'Silin, s. f. a cherry', 'Silis', and 'Silleadh, s. the countenance; a turning; looking' (with ZERO *sileabhar anywhere in the dictionary or O'Donovan's Supplement!). Real Irish neighbors either fail phonologically against shillaber — silleadh (SLTK vs SLPL = 0.5000), siollaire ('verse-scanner, carper', SL vs SLPL = 0.5000), sileastar ('sedge', SLSTL vs SLPL = 0.4000) — or have purely agricultural semantics unrelated to carnival/auction decoys (síoladóir /ˈʃiːl̪ˠəd̪ˠoːɾʲ/ 'agricultural seed-sower').
